ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In "children's bungee jumping," what are tied to the left and right sides of the waist are rubber ropes with excellent elasticity. When Xiao Ming, whose mass is m, is suspended at rest as shown in the figure, the magnitudes of the tensions in the two rubber ropes are both exactly mg. If at this moment the rubber rope on Xiao Ming's right side breaks at the waist, then what are the magnitude and direction of Xiao Ming's acceleration at this moment?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The acceleration a = g, obliquely downward along the direction of the originally broken rubber rope
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, Xiao Ming (the child) is suspended in the air, with one obliquely upward rubber rope connected to each of the left and right sides of his waist; beside the rubber rope on the right side there is the label "this rope breaks," indicating that the rope connected to Xiao Ming's right waist breaks. Then reason: Before the break, Xiao Ming is at rest, so the forces are balanced, and the vector sum of the left-rope tension, the right-rope tension, and gravity is zero, that is, T_left + T_right + mg = 0. The problem states that before the two ropes break, the magnitudes of their tensions are both mg. At the instant when the right-side rubber rope breaks at the waist, only the tension exerted by the right rope on Xiao Ming is removed; because the instantaneous position has not yet had time to change, the left-rope tension and gravity can be regarded as still maintaining the values at the instant before the break. Therefore the resultant force after the break is T_left + mg = -T_right. The original tension magnitude of the right rope was mg, so the magnitude of the resultant force after the break is mg, and its direction is opposite to the original tension direction of the right rope, that is, obliquely downward along the direction of the originally broken rubber rope. By Newton's second law, a = F_resultant/m = mg/m = g.
